sections.title: CONCEPT EXPLANATION (Junior Developer Style)
sections.body:
A **string** in Python is a sequence of characters enclosed in quotes. Think of it like a **necklace of beads** — each bead is a character, and together they form a word, sentence, or any text.

```
"Hello"
 H e l l o
 0 1 2 3 4   ← Each character has a position (index)
```

### 🔑 Key Characteristics of Python Strings:

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| **Immutable** | Once created, cannot be changed in-place |
| **Ordered** | Characters maintain their position |
| **Iterable** | You can loop through each character |
| **Indexed** | Access any character by position |
| **Any Unicode** | Supports all languages, emojis, symbols |

### 📌 Immutability — The Most Important Property!
```python
name = "Alice"
name[0] = "B"   # ❌ TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

# Strings CANNOT be modified — you create a NEW string instead!
name = "B" + name[1:]   # ✅ Creates new string "Blice"
```

### 🏠 Real World Analogy:
Think of a string like a **printed book page** — you can READ any letter by its position, but you can't erase and rewrite a letter on the page. You'd need to **print a new page** with the change.

### When to Use Strings?
- Storing names, emails, messages, URLs
- Processing text data (logs, CSV files, JSON)
- User input and output
- Template generation (HTML, SQL, emails)

sections.title: 5 EXAMPLES
sections.body:
### Example 1: String Basics — Creation and Type
```python
# All valid ways to create strings
s1 = 'Hello'                    # Single quotes
s2 = "World"                    # Double quotes
s3 = '''Multi
line'''                         # Triple single quotes
s4 = """Also
multi-line"""                   # Triple double quotes
s5 = str(12345)                 # Convert number to string
s6 = str(True)                  # Convert bool to string

print(type(s1))                 # <class 'str'>
print(type(s5))                 # <class 'str'>
print(s5)                       # "12345"
print(s6)                       # "True"

# Check if something is a string
print(isinstance(s1, str))      # True
print(isinstance(42, str))      # False

# String length
print(len("Hello World"))       # 11 (spaces count!)
print(len(""))                  # 0 — empty string
print(len("नमस्ते"))            # 6 — Unicode works!
```

### Example 2: Immutability in Action
```python
# Demonstrating immutability
name = "Veerababu"

# ❌ This FAILS — strings are immutable
try:
    name[0] = "v"
except TypeError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
# Error: 'str' object does not support item assignment

# ✅ Create a NEW string instead
name_lower = name[0].lower() + name[1:]
print(name_lower)               # veerababu

# ✅ Reassigning the variable is fine
name = "Veerababu Kumar"        # This creates a NEW string object
print(name)

# Proof of immutability with id()
s = "hello"
original_id = id(s)
s = s + " world"               # New string, new memory address!
print(id(s) == original_id)    # False — different object!
```

### Example 3: Strings as Sequences
```python
message = "Python"

# Strings are sequences — support sequence operations
print(len(message))             # 6
print(message[0])               # P — first character
print(message[-1])              # n — last character
print(message[1:4])             # yth — slicing

# Iterate through characters
print("Characters in 'Python':")
for char in message:
    print(f"  '{char}'", end="")
print()

# Check membership
print("P" in message)           # True
print("z" in message)           # False
print("yth" in message)         # True — works for substrings too!

# Count characters
print(message.count("o"))       # 1
print("mississippi".count("ss")) # 2
```

### Example 4: String Identity vs Equality
```python
# == checks VALUE (content)
# is  checks IDENTITY (same object in memory)

s1 = "hello"
s2 = "hello"
s3 = "".join(["h","e","l","l","o"])

print(s1 == s2)         # True  — same content
print(s1 == s3)         # True  — same content

# Python interns short strings (optimization)
print(s1 is s2)         # True  — Python reuses same object (interning)
print(s1 is s3)         # False — dynamically created string

# ⚠️ ALWAYS use == for string comparison!
# Never use 'is' to compare string values
user_input = input("Enter name: ") if False else "Veerababu"
if user_input == "Veerababu":    # ✅ Correct
    print("Welcome!")
# Never: if user_input is "Veerababu"  ← unreliable!
```

### Example 5: Real-World String Usage
```python
# Building a user profile string
first_name = "Veerababu"
last_name  = "Kumar"
age        = 26
city       = "Hyderabad"
email      = "veerababu@example.com"

# Create various string representations
full_name   = first_name + " " + last_name
greeting    = f"Hello, {full_name}!"
profile_url = f"https://app.com/users/{first_name.lower()}"
display     = f"[{age}] {full_name} — {city}"
masked_email= email[:3] + "***" + email[email.index("@"):]

print(greeting)         # Hello, Veerababu Kumar!
print(profile_url)      # https://app.com/users/veerababu
print(display)          # [26] Veerababu Kumar — Hyderabad
print(masked_email)     # vee***@example.com
print(f"Name length: {len(full_name)} chars")  # 15 chars
```

quiz.explanation: 5-Year Experience Answer: "String immutability means once a string object is created in memory, its content cannot be changed. Any operation that appears to 'modify' a string actually creates a brand new string object. For example, s = s + ' world' doesn't append to the existing string — it allocates new memory for the combined result and rebinds the variable s to the new object.

quiz.explanation: 5-Year Experience Answer: "Python 3 strings are Unicode by default — they can store any character from any language. Internally, CPython uses a flexible string representation (PEP 393): it uses 1, 2, or 4 bytes per character depending on the largest code point in the string — Latin-only strings use 1 byte per char, BMP characters use 2 bytes, emojis/rare chars use 4 bytes. This is very memory-efficient.
